results.title: Thousands March in Athens to Mark 1973 Uprising Against Military Dictatorship
results.description: The anniversary commemorates the November 1973 uprising at Athens Polytechnic, when students occupied the university demanding democracy and an end to military rule. Thousands of Greeks marched through central Athens on Tuesday to commemorate the 53rd anniversary of the 1973 student uprising against the country's military dictatorship, in a largely peaceful demonstration that ended with clashes between protesters and police. Police estimated that about 20,000 people participated in the annual march to the U.S. Embassy, a politically charged tradition reflecting Washington's historical support for Greece's military regime, which ruled from 1967 to 1974. The anniversary commemorates the November 1973 uprising at Athens Polytechnic, when students occupied the university demanding democracy and an end to military rule. The regime sent troops and tanks to crush the revolt, which became a defining symbol of resistance and helped undermine the dictatorship. Demonstrators carried a bloodstained Greek flag associated with the uprising, while student organizations, labor unions and opposition parties marched behind banners calling for democracy and social justice. The main procession concluded shortly after 8:30 p.m. without major incidents along its route. Violence erupted afterward near Alexandras Avenue, where riot police used chemical irritants against groups attempting to approach Athens police headquarters. Witnesses alleged that an officer struck a female demonstrator in the head with a riot shield. Local media reported that four women suffered head injuries and were taken to a hospital. Police also entered the Ambelokipi subway station and detained several people, including a minor, prompting protests from passengers and bystanders. Authorities reported 15 detentions in Athens, two of which resulted in arrests. A female police officer was also injured by a stone during security checks earlier in the day. Smaller confrontations occurred near Klafthmonos Square, where protesters threw stones and incendiary devices. Demonstrations also took place in Thessaloniki, Greece's second-largest city, where protesters burned an American flag and gathered outside the U.S. Consulate. Marches were held in Patras, with additional detentions reported. The anniversary remains one of Greece's most politically significant commemorations, bringing together generations of protesters and serving as a reminder of the country's struggle to restore democracy. More than five decades later, the annual march continues to reflect tensions over political freedoms, policing and Greece's relationship with the United States. #ATHENS #MARCH #MILITARY

results.title: Gujarat riots survivor Bilkis Bano 'heartbroken' after two of her rapists granted bail
results.description: NEW DELHI — A pregnant Muslim woman who was gang-raped and saw 14 family members murdered during the 2002 Gujarat riots has spoken of her "shock and disbelief" after the Supreme Court granted bail to two of her rapists and suspended their life sentences. Bilkis Bano said in a statement that the top court passed the order without hearing her and that she heard about the court order through press reports. The freed men are from a group of 11 convicts, part of a Hindu mob, serving life terms for the attack on Bano. All the men were also freed in 2022 after a Gujarat government order. That decision, and the celebrations as they left prison, caused global outrage. In 2024, the Supreme Court overturned the order. In a short three-page order dated 28 October, the Supreme Court granted bail to Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya and suspended their sentences while their petition challenging a 2017 Bombay High Court order is being heard. The judges explained that the early release was because the two convicts "have been under incarceration for a period of more than 17 years" and "that one of the appellants has a severe handicap".On Tuesday, Bano's lawyer Shobha Gupta told the BBC that the news of Joshi and Modhiya's release had left "Bilkis heartbroken"."She has to restart her battle for justice. She had no information that this case was coming up in the Supreme Court. What is troubling for us is that every time something like this happens, we worry that it could affect her faith in judiciary."Gupta said it was difficult to understand why the convicts were being released because "it's not a routine criminal case, it's a case that shocks the conscience of the world, of entire humanity".The attack on Bano and her family was one of the most horrific crimes during the Gujarat riots, which began after 60 Hindu pilgrims were killed in a fire on a passenger train in the town of Godhra. Hindu mobs attacked Muslim neighborhoods, blaming them for starting the fire. The riots continued for three days and more than 2,000 people died, most of them Muslims. When rioters attacked Bano's village and started setting Muslim homes on fire, she and 16 relatives went on the run. She was 19, had a three-year-old daughter and was pregnant with her second child. They were attacked on the morning of 3 March 2002 by a group of men "with swords and sticks", she told me in 2017. Her three-year-old daughter, she said, was snatched from her lap and killed. Her attackers were her neighbours, men she had seen almost daily while growing up. They tore off her clothes and several of them raped her, ignoring her pleas for mercy. Her cousin, who had given birth two days earlier, was raped and murdered and her newborn baby was killed too. Bano survived only because she lost consciousness and her attackers left, believing she was dead. Two boys - seven and four - were the only other survivors of the massacre. Her fight for justice has been long and nightmarish. The first arrests were made only in 2004 after the Supreme Court called in federal investigators and transferred her case to Mumbai, saying that courts in Gujarat could not deliver justice to her. In her statement released on Monday night, Bano spoke of "fresh tears of pain, shock and disbelief"."I still cannot believe that once again, for the second time, an order has been passed by the Supreme Court without calling me up and without hearing me," she said."For 24 long years, I have stood up to fight for justice... again and again. Yet today, I find myself losing the very justice I had fought so hard to win.... And I am scared of losing faith in justice, yet again."Bano vowed to "fight this order... for my children, who do not deserve to live haunted by fears and scars for the rest of their lives"."I do this for my three-year-old Saleha who deserved to live and whose memory demands justice. I do this for women everywhere. Because no woman, no survivor, no citizen should have to endure this eternal test of belonging and equality, and fight for justice for the rest of her life."Prime Minister Narendra Modi was Gujarat chief minister at the time of the riots, and was criticised for not doing enough to prevent the carnage. He has always denied wrongdoing and has not apologised for the riots. In 2013, a Supreme Court panel also said that there was insufficient evidence to prosecute him. But critics have continued to blame him for the riots happening on his watch.
